Content:
In previous lessons, we saw how to define the limit of a null sequence (i.e., a sequence whose limit equals zero) and how to construct a formal proof that a given sequence is null.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include sequences that converge a finite (not necessarily zero) limit. If such a limit exists, it's usually denoted as [MATH: L.]

Content:
Consider the following sequence:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n+1}{n}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
It's easy to see that the limit of this sequence is [MATH: {\color{red}{L}}={\color{red}{1}}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((n + 1)/(n)); = lim_(n → ∞)((n)/(n) + (1)/(n)); = lim_(n → ∞)(1 + (1)/(n)); = 1 + 0; = 1]

Content:
This means that for any [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] there exists a natural number [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] such that the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: {\color{red}{L}} = {\color{red}{1}}] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.] In other words,

Content:
[MATH: \forall n\geq N,\qquad|a_n - {\color{red}{1}}| < \varepsilon.]

Content:
Let's draw a few sketches to illustrate this idea.

Content:
- If we select [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.5,] then [MATH: |a_n-{\color{red}{1}}| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n \geq 3.]

Content:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/35327b468df8bdbdae1e5fcf2151ba97]

Content:
- If [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.1,] then [MATH: |a_n-{\color{red}{1}}| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n \geq 11.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/35c1c6db6967cd0e00933d3d75832a21]

Content:
The key idea is this: By making [MATH: \varepsilon] smaller and smaller, we can always find an index [MATH: N] where the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: \color{red}L] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

Content:
Based on the discussion so far, the notation
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = {\color{red}{L}}]
means that if we take any arbitrarily small positive number [MATH: \varepsilon,] the distance of each [MATH: a_n] from [MATH: {\color{red}{L}}] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for sufficiently large [MATH: n.]

Content:
This gives us our definition of a finite limit:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| a_n-L \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:

Graphic:

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{n+1}{n}\right) = {\color{red}{1}}]
means the following:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have
> [MATH: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
We can make this definition more formal by explicitly including an implication:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] if [MATH: n\geq N,] then
> [MATH: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
[MATH: \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon]

sections.normalized_html:
We need to find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that

[MATH: \left| \dfrac{5^n+1}{5^n+6}- 1 \right| < 0.001]

for all [MATH: n \geq N.]

First, simplifying [MATH: |a_n - L|,] we have

[MATH: |a_{n} − L||=|(5^{n} + 1)/(5^{n} + 6) − 1|; =|(5^{n} + 1)/(5^{n} + 6) − (5^{n} + 6)/(5^{n} + 6)|; =|(5^{n} + 1 − 5^{n} − 6)/(5^{n} + 6)|; =|(− 5)/(5^{n} + 6)|; =|− (5)/(5^{n} + 6)|.]

Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{5}{5^n+6} > 0] for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1.] With that in mind, we have

[MATH: |a_n - L| = \left|- \dfrac{5}{5^n+6} \right| = \dfrac{5}{5^n+6}.]

Now, we solve the following inequality for [MATH: n{:}]

[MATH: (5)/(5^{n} + 6)|< 0.001; 5|< 0.001(5^{n} + 6); (5)/(0.001)|< 5^{n} + 6; (5)/(0.001) − 6|< 5^{n}; 4994|< 5^{n}; \log_{5} (4994)|< n; n|> \log_{5} (4994) ≈ 5.291]

As a result, [MATH: \left| \dfrac{5^n+1}{5^n+6}- 1 \right| < 0.001] for all natural numbers [MATH: n \geq \lceil 5.291 \rceil = 6.]

Therefore, [MATH: N = 6.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In previous lessons, we saw how to define the limit of a null sequence (i.e., a sequence whose limit equals zero) and how to construct a formal proof that a given sequence is null.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include sequences that converge a finite (not necessarily zero) limit. If such a limit exists, it's usually denoted as [MATH: L.]

Content:
Consider the following sequence:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n+1}{n}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
It's easy to see that the limit of this sequence is [MATH: {\color{red}{L}}={\color{red}{1}}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((n + 1)/(n)); = lim_(n → ∞)((n)/(n) + (1)/(n)); = lim_(n → ∞)(1 + (1)/(n)); = 1 + 0; = 1]

Content:
This means that for any [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] there exists a natural number [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] such that the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: {\color{red}{L}} = {\color{red}{1}}] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.] In other words,

Content:
[MATH: \forall n\geq N,\qquad|a_n - {\color{red}{1}}| < \varepsilon.]

Content:
Let's draw a few sketches to illustrate this idea.

The key idea is this: By making [MATH: \varepsilon] smaller and smaller, we can always find an index [MATH: N] where the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: \color{red}L] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Formal Definition of a Finite Limit

Content:
Based on the discussion so far, the notation
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = {\color{red}{L}}]
means that if we take any arbitrarily small positive number [MATH: \varepsilon,] the distance of each [MATH: a_n] from [MATH: {\color{red}{L}}] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for sufficiently large [MATH: n.]

Content:
This gives us our definition of a finite limit:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| a_n-L \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
We can illustrate the key idea using the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afa5bb26334cb12ef6d9bbc6899d2af7]

Content:
For example, the statement

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{n+1}{n}\right) = {\color{red}{1}}]
means the following:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have
> [MATH: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
We can make this definition more formal by explicitly including an implication:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] if [MATH: n\geq N,] then
> [MATH: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
Finally, by expressing the last statement using formal symbolic notation, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{n+1}{n}-{\color{red}{1}} \right| \lt \varepsilon]
